'''''Caesaria templaria''''' is an [[extinct]] species of [[Stem group|stem]]-turtle in the [[testudinata]]n clade [[Thalassochelydia]], known from the [[Late Jurassic]] ([[Tithonian]] age) [[Canjuers Lagerstätte]] of France. ''C. templaria'' is the [[Monotypic taxon|only species]] in the genus '''''Caesaria''''', known from two specimens preserving the shell and skull.

== Discovery and naming ==
[[File:Caesaria templaria (referred, MNHN.F.CNJ174).jpg|thumb|upright|Referred specimen under natural (A) and [[UV]] light (C), and in [[false color]] (D)]]
The first ''Caesaria'' fossil material was discovered during excavations by the Ghirardi family between 1965 and 1971. The Ghirardis had begun quarrying for ornamental stone on land they owned near the 'Les Bessons' camp area in [[Var (department)|Var]], southeastern France, when they incidentally discovered a [[Lagerstätte]] site (now called the [[Canjuers Lagerstätte]]) preserving diverse fossils of plants, invertebrates, and vertebrates.<ref name="Peyer2014" /> These rocks represent outcrops of the [[Calcaire Blancs de Provence Formation|'Calcaire Blancs de Provence' Formation]]. In 1983, the [[National Museum of Natural History, France|National Museum of Natural History]] (MNHN) in Paris purchased part of the Ghirardis' private collection, and it is now permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] here. Among these fossils is specimen MNHN.F.CNJ77, a nearly complete turtle skeleton on a single slab. The skull and shell are preserved in their entirety, in addition to some partial [[cervical vertebrae|cervical (neck) vertebrae]] and fragmentary limb bones. The Ghirardis did not record or share the exact [[stratigraphic]] positions of the specimens they collected, though the rock slabs on which the fossils are preserved indicate they derived from [[lithographic limestone]] strata.<ref name="Spicher26" />

Specimen MNHN.F.CNJ174, independently collected from this region during an excavation led by MNHN paleontologist S. Wenz, was integrated into the museum's collections alongside the Ghirardi collection in 1983. It comprises an inferiorly preserved skeleton, with much of the shell and some components of the skull.<ref name="Spicher26" /> In 1994, French paleontologist France de Lapparent de Broin published a preliminary review of three Canjuers turtle specimens from the Ghirardi collection, in which she identified MNHN.F.CNJ77 as an indeterminate species of he genus ''[[Eurysternum]]''.<ref name="Broin1994" /> MNHN.F.CNJ174 remained undescribed.<ref name="Spicher26" />

In 2026, Gaël E. Spicher and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Caesaria templaria'' as a new genus and species of extinct turtle based on these fossil remains, designating MNHN.F.CNJ77 as the [[holotype]] specimen. MNHN.F.CNJ174 was referred to this species, receiving its first full anatomical description. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Caesaria'', is an indirect reference to the [[Type locality (biology)|type locality]] of ''C. templaria''; the [[Canjuers]] plateau was, in antiquity, referred to as Campus Julii ({{lit|plain of [[Julius Caesar]]}}), referencing Caesar's passage through the region during the [[Gallic Wars]]. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''templaria'', references the medieval [[Knights Templar|Templar]] stronghold in [[Comps-sur-Artuby]], a village near the Les Bessons area.<ref name="Spicher26" />
